passages.t: Faithful in God's house: Moses the servant, Jesus the Son
passages.happening:
“Therefore, holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling, set your focus on Jesus, the apostle and high priest whom we confess” (verse 1).

The writer now sets Jesus beside Moses. “He was faithful to the One who appointed Him, just as Moses was faithful in all God’s house” (verse 2). Both were faithful. But Jesus has more honour, “just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself. And every house is built by someone, but God is the builder of everything” (verses 3-4).

“Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house, testifying to what would be spoken later. But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house. And we are His house, if we hold firmly to our confidence and the hope of which we boast” (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
‘Holy brothers’ means all the believers, men and women, set apart for God. They ‘share in the heavenly calling’: God has called them to a home that is not yet theirs.

‘Set your focus’ means look hard and keep looking. The readers were tired and distracted. The cure is to fix their minds on Jesus.

Jesus is called ‘apostle’ here, the only place in the New Testament where he is. An apostle is someone sent. Jesus is the one God sent to us, and the high priest who goes to God for us. ‘Whom we confess’ may point to words the church said together, perhaps at baptism.

For the first readers no one in Israel's past stood higher than Moses. Through him God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave the law. Many Jewish writings of the time spoke of him with the greatest honour. So the writer is careful. He begins by saying that Moses was faithful, as God himself said. Then he uses a picture. A ‘house’ meant both a building and a household: the family, the servants and the property. Moses was a trusted servant in God's household. The word used for ‘servant’ is not the plain word for a slave but a word for an honoured attendant. Jesus is the Son, the heir, over the household. And God's ‘house’ is his people. ‘We are His house.’
passages.ot:
The words about Moses come from Numbers 12. When Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, God defended him. To other prophets God spoke in visions and dreams, “But this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house” (Numbers 12:7). God himself gave Moses this honour, and Hebrews repeats it.

At the end of the Law, Moses is honoured again: “Since that time, no prophet has risen in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face” (Deuteronomy 34:10).

Moses also pointed beyond himself: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Hebrews says Moses was ‘testifying to what would be spoken later’. His whole work bore witness ahead of itself.
passages.hard:
Is Hebrews putting Moses down, and through him the law and the Jewish faith?

No. Read the verses slowly. The first thing the writer says about Moses is that he was faithful, using God's own words about him from Numbers 12:7. He compares Jesus with Moses not because Moses was small, but because he was so great. If you want to show how high someone is, you compare him with the highest person your readers know. For a Jewish believer, that was Moses.

The contrast is between a faithful servant and a son, both in the same house, both serving the same God. It is not between a false religion and a true one. Moses' work was God's work, and it pointed forward to what God would say in his Son.

For centuries some Christians used this letter, with other parts of the New Testament, to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why, and the book page's part on the old covenant and the Jewish people says more.

And notice the warning at the end of verse 6. The writer does not say, ‘they’ are out and ‘we’ are in. He says ‘we’ are God's house ‘if we hold firmly’. The warning is aimed at believers in Jesus, the writer included.
passages.asks: Moses was faithful as a servant; Jesus as the Son. Ask where you need to ‘set your focus’ on Jesus today, instead of on what tires you. Ask whether you honour those who served God faithfully before you. And ask what it means to belong to a house that God is building, and that you are part of.

passages.t: ‘Today, if you hear His voice’: Psalm 95
passages.happening:
The writer now quotes a psalm, and he introduces it as God speaking now: “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says” (verse 7).

“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion, in the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers tested and tried Me, and for forty years saw My works. Therefore I was angry with that generation, and I said, ‘Their hearts are always going astray, and they have not known My ways.’ So I swore on oath in My anger, ‘They shall never enter My rest.’” (verses 7-11).
passages.hearers:
The writer moves from Moses to the people Moses led. They had been rescued from Egypt. They were on the way to the promised land. And many of them never arrived. The readers were in the same place: rescued by Christ, on the way, not yet home. The psalm is a mirror.

‘As the Holy Spirit says’ is in the present tense. For the writer, Scripture is not only something God once said. God says it now, to these readers, and to us.

‘Harden your hearts’ means to make yourself stiff and unwilling, so that God's word no longer gets in. It is the language used of Pharaoh in the exodus. A heart does not usually harden in a day. It hardens by saying no again and again.

‘My rest’ was, first of all, the promised land, a home after slavery and wandering. Chapter 4 will show that God's rest means even more than that.
passages.ot:
Verses 7 to 11 quote Psalm 95:7-11. The psalm begins as a joyful call to worship, “Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD” (Psalm 95:1), and ends with this warning from God.

In the Hebrew, as the Berean Standard Bible has it, the psalm names two places: “do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness” (Psalm 95:8). Massah means ‘testing’ and Meribah means ‘quarrelling’. They were names for the place where the people, thirsty, “tested the LORD, saying, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’” (Exodus 17:7). The Greek Old Testament, which Hebrews quotes, translated the names by their meaning, so Hebrews has ‘the rebellion’ and ‘the day of testing’.

There is one more small difference. In the psalm, the forty years go with God's anger: “For forty years I was angry with that generation” (Psalm 95:10). In Hebrews the words are arranged so that the forty years go with what the people saw: they ‘for forty years saw My works’. Both are true. They saw God's care for forty years, and they kept testing him. Later, in verse 17, Hebrews uses the psalm's own order.

The oath of verse 11 looks back to Numbers 14. When the people refused to enter the land, God said that none of that generation would see it (Numbers 14:22-23). “How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?” (Numbers 14:11).
passages.hard:
Does ‘They shall never enter My rest’ mean God rejected Israel?

No. The oath was about one generation, the adults who refused to enter the land at Kadesh. In the same chapter God says, “I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected—and they will enjoy it” (Numbers 14:31). Their children did enter, led by Joshua. “And the LORD gave them rest on every side, just as He had sworn to their fathers” (Joshua 21:44).

The psalm itself was sung in Israel's worship as a warning to Israel's own worshippers, so that they would not repeat the past. Hebrews does the same for a congregation of believers in Jesus. The warning is aimed at ‘us’, not at anyone else. Paul uses the same wilderness story in the same way: “these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

And God's anger in the psalm is not a bad temper. It is the anger of one who had cared for his people for forty years and was refused again and again. The Bible never treats it lightly, and it never says it is God's last word for those who turn back to him.
passages.asks: ‘Today, if you hear His voice.’ Ask whether God has been saying something to you that you keep putting off. Ask where your heart has grown stiff by small refusals. And ask what you have seen of God's care, perhaps for many years, that you need to remember when you are tempted to doubt him.

passages.happening:
Now the writer applies the psalm to his readers.

“See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God. But exhort one another daily, as long as it is called today, so that none of you may be hardened by sin’s deceitfulness” (verses 12-13).

“We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end the assurance we had at first” (verse 14).

He repeats the opening of the psalm: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
‘See to it’ means keep watching. The danger is ‘a wicked heart of unbelief’: not a mind with questions, but a heart that turns away from the living God. ‘The living God’ means God is not an idea or an idol. He is alive, and he is the one a person would be leaving.

The cure is not each person trying harder alone. It is ‘exhort one another daily’. The first readers probably met in homes, in small groups where people knew each other well. They could notice when someone was growing cold, and speak to them. In this letter, holding on is something believers do together.

‘As long as it is called today’ turns the word ‘Today’ from the psalm into a name for the whole present time. Now is the time to listen. Now is the time to help one another.

‘Sin’s deceitfulness’ pictures sin as a liar. It promises what it cannot give, and little by little it hardens the heart.

‘We have come to share in Christ’ means we belong to him, as his companions, already. ‘If we hold firmly to the end’ adds the call to keep going.
passages.ot:
The writer reads Psalm 95 as a warning to his own congregation, as Israel's worshippers did when they sang it. Its picture of hardening has a sad history in the Old Testament. At the exodus the LORD said, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 7:3), and Pharaoh hardened his own heart too. And when the people grumbled in the desert they asked Moses, “Why have you brought us out of Egypt—to make us and our children and livestock die of thirst?” (Exodus 17:3), though they had just seen God open the sea.

The call to encourage one another fits the Old Testament's picture of a people who keep faith together: “As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another” (Proverbs 27:17).
passages.hard:
‘We have come to share in Christ if we hold firmly to the end’ (verse 14). Does this mean a believer can lose their salvation?

Christians read this verse in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition notice its order: ‘we have come to share’ is something already done, and holding firm shows that it is real. On this reading, keeping on is the evidence that someone truly belongs to Christ, not the way to earn it, and those who finally turn away show that they never truly belonged. Many Arminian and Wesleyan readers take the condition at face value, as a real danger for real believers, who can harden their hearts and lose what they had. Others hold that warnings like this are the very means God uses to keep his people faithful: the danger is real, and so is God's promise to keep those who listen. These notes do not choose. The site's note on Romans 8:31-39 sets out both main views, and so does the Honest Answer, ‘Can you lose your salvation?’

All of these readings take the warning seriously. And all of them hear the writer's cure in verse 13: do not try to hold on alone.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Holding on is something believers do together. Ask who you know well enough to notice if you were growing cold, and who you would notice. Ask whether there is someone you could encourage this week. And ask where sin has been lying to you, promising what it cannot give.

passages.t: They could not enter because of unbelief
passages.happening:
The writer asks three questions about the wilderness generation and answers each with another question.

“For who were the ones who heard and rebelled? Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt?” (verse 16).

“And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?” (verse 17).

“And to whom did He swear that they would never enter His rest? Was it not to those who disobeyed?” (verse 18).

Then the answer: “So we see that it was because of their unbelief that they were unable to enter” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The questions make a sobering point. The people who failed were not strangers to God. They were the very people God had rescued. They had walked out of Egypt. They had seen the sea open. They had eaten the manna. And still they did not trust him.

The writer joins two words: ‘disobeyed’ (verse 18) and ‘unbelief’ (verse 19). In the Greek the word for ‘disobey’ can also mean ‘refuse to believe’. The two belong together. Not trusting God shows itself in not following him.

‘Unable to enter’: their unbelief closed the door. God had not stopped wanting to give them the land. They refused to go in.

For the readers, the point was plain. Having started well does not take the place of keeping on. They too had been rescued. They too were on the way.
passages.ot:
The questions retell Numbers 14. At Kadesh, after the spies came back from Canaan, the people refused to go in and wanted to go back to Egypt. God's sentence was, “Your bodies will fall in this wilderness—all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older—because you have grumbled against Me” (Numbers 14:29). Only Caleb and Joshua, who had trusted God, would enter (Numbers 14:30).

The same story is retold in the psalms: “they did not believe His promise. They grumbled in their tents” (Psalm 106:24-25).

And the Law itself looked ahead to a rest still to come: “For you have not yet come to the resting place and the inheritance that the LORD your God is giving you” (Deuteronomy 12:9). Chapter 4 picks up that thought.
passages.asks: The people who fell had seen great things. Ask whether you are leaning on what God did for you long ago, instead of trusting him now. Ask where unbelief in your life shows itself as not following. And ask what it would mean to take the next step God is asking of you, instead of turning back.
